vopros: Should I pay for a tool that tracks whether ChatGPT and other AI assistants mention my business, or hire someone to get my business recommended by AI?

vyzhimka.tekst:
Potentially, but I’d separate the two purchases. “AI visibility tracking” and “getting recommended by AI” are different jobs, and the second is much harder to measure.

AI assistants are becoming genuine discovery channels. OpenAI says ChatGPT shopping uses merchant data, public product information, and retail sources to generate recommendations; Google has dedicated guidance and reporting for visibility in its generative AI features; Microsoft now has an AI Performance report showing citations in Copilot and related experiences. ([openai.com](https://openai.com/index/powering-product-discovery-in-chatgpt/?utm_source=openai))

For most small or midsize businesses, I would approach spending in this order:

- First, establish whether AI recommendations could materially generate customers for you. Make a list of 20–50 prompts a prospective customer might genuinely ask, such as “best wedding photographer in Pasadena,” “good accounting software for a 10-person construction company,” or “best ergonomic office chair under $500.” Test several assistants and record who appears.
- Second, fix the fundamentals before buying a sophisticated monitoring platform. Your business, products/services, location, pricing, differentiators, and reputation need to be clearly represented on your own site and on authoritative third-party sources. Google explicitly says its existing SEO fundamentals remain relevant to its generative AI systems; Microsoft gives similar guidance. ([developers.google.com](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features?utm_source=openai))
- Third, use first-party measurement wherever possible. Google now provides generative-AI visibility reporting in Search Console, while Bing Webmaster Tools reports citations and queries associated with AI answers. Those won't tell you everything happening inside every assistant, but they're valuable data you don't need an expensive GEO platform to obtain. ([developers.google.com](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/06/gen-ai-performance-reports?utm_source=openai))
- Then consider a tracking tool if AI visibility has become important enough that manually testing prompts is cumbersome. Its value is primarily benchmarking: share of mentions, competitors, prompts where you're absent, citations/sources, and changes over time. Treat the resulting “AI visibility score” as a directional metric rather than ground truth; responses can vary with wording, model, context, location, and time.
- Hire someone only if they're going to improve the underlying signals—not merely sell “GEO optimization.” Useful work can include technical SEO, creating genuinely useful comparison/category/service content, cleaning up product or business data, earning credible third-party coverage/reviews, and measuring resulting leads or sales.

I'd be especially skeptical of anyone promising “we'll get ChatGPT to recommend you.” There isn't a magic piece of schema, an `llms.txt` file, or a secret submission trick that guarantees recommendations. Google specifically says there are no special AI-search technical requirements or special schema beyond normal search fundamentals, and warns that third-party AEO/GEO services don't have access to Google's internal ranking data and can't guarantee performance. Microsoft similarly states GEO cannot guarantee citations. ([developers.google.com](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features?utm_source=openai))

There are exceptions. If you're an e-commerce company, I'd pay more attention now because AI platforms are building direct product-discovery infrastructure. For example, OpenAI says Shopify catalog data is integrated into ChatGPT product discovery and also supports merchant feeds through its Agentic Commerce Protocol. ([openai.com](https://openai.com/index/powering-product-discovery-in-chatgpt/?utm_source=openai))

So if you gave me, say, a $1,000/month experimental budget, I wouldn't immediately put $500 into a tracker and $500 into a “GEO agency.” I'd first spend a modest amount measuring a fixed set of high-commercial-intent prompts, then put most of the money into fixing whatever explains why competitors are being selected over you. Tracking only becomes worth much money when you have enough AI-generated business that knowing whether your visibility moved from X to Y affects an actual decision.

If you tell me what kind of business you have (and roughly how much a new customer is worth), I can tell you whether I'd spend $0, a few hundred dollars, or several thousand a month on this.
